Place and dates of trial:                      Vancouver,
B.C.

April
5-8 and 15, 1994

Jalal Zangana and Ingrid Benz are
the biological or "birth"  parents of an infant I will call baby
Ingrid.  Baby Ingrid was born in British Columbia on July 7, 1993.  Eleven days
after her birth, Ingrid Benz signed the necessary papers to allow baby Ingrid
to be placed for private adoption with John and Margaret Doe.  The Does were
selected by Ms. Benz as adoptive parents for baby Ingrid with the assistance of
the Hope Pregnancy and Adoption Services Society.  Baby Ingrid has been cared
for by John and Margaret Doe since July 21, 1993.  They wish to retain custody
of her and plan to apply to adopt her.

Jalal Zangana learned of baby
Ingrid's birth and that she had been placed for adoption in August of 1993, but
Ingrid Benz refused to tell Mr. Zangana where the baby was, or the name of the
adoptive parents.  Mr. Zangana commenced a lawsuit in Winnipeg, Manitoba, where
he and Ms. Benz live, to compel Ms. Benz to disclose the whereabouts of baby
Ingrid.  Through those proceedings, Mr. Zangana learned that baby Ingrid was in
British Columbia, with the Does.  In January, 1994, he commenced this proceeding,
seeking custody of baby Ingrid.  The Does seek to retain custody, and they
oppose Mr. Zangana's alternative application for access.  Ingrid Benz supports
the Does' claim for custody, but says that if the Does are not permitted to
retain custody of baby Ingrid, it would be in the child's best interests for
Ms. Benz to have custody, instead of Mr. Zangana.

FACTS

Mr. Zangana was born in Iraq.  He
is 39 years old.  He is of Kurdish descent, and was ordered to leave Iraq when
he was a university student after a conflict with a professor.  He was deported
to Damascus and then settled in Egypt.  In Egypt he married, but his wife died
of kidney disease in 1985, after they had been married five years.  In 1989 Mr.
Zangana immigrated to Canada as a refugee, settling in Winnipeg.  He became a
Canadian citizen on November 5, 1992.  One of Mr. Zangana's brothers lives in
Sweden, his parents and other siblings live in Iraq.  They are financially
well-off, according to Mr. Zangana's evidence.

Since arriving in Canada, Mr.
Zangana has worked as a taxi driver in Winnipeg, Manitoba.  Since January, 1994
Mr. Zangana has been staying in Vancouver in order to conduct these
proceedings, and he is currently unemployed but has employment available to him
as a taxi driver when he returns to Winnipeg.

Ms. Benz is 37 years old.  She
was born in Germany but immigrated to Canada with her family when she was three
years old.  She became a Canadian citizen in 1977.  She grew up in a small town
near Kenora, Ontario, and completed Grade 12.  She started driving a taxi-cab
in Winnipeg in 1975, and also worked as a taxi dispatcher for a few months.  In
1980 she bought her own taxi and worked as an owner-operator until 1984, when
she sold the taxi.  She says she needed a rest; that being a successful
owner-operator involved working 12 hours a day, seven days a week.  She took
four or five months off.  When she returned to work, she began driving taxi
part-time for Unicity Taxi in Winnipeg.  She also started up a small business
she called "The Garment Doctor", doing clothing alterations.  She
worked at this on a part-time basis, until sometime after she met Mr. Zangana
in 1991.

Mr. Zangana and Ms. Benz met in
June or July, 1991, at the taxi company for which they both worked at the
time.  Their relationship developed quickly.  In September, 1991 Ms. Benz was
living in a friend's townhouse.  With the friend's permission, Mr. Zangana
moved in with Ms. Benz.  Mr. Zangana and Ms. Benz discussed marriage.  Ms. Benz
says she wanted to marry Mr. Zangana and have children with him.  Mr. Zangana
produced a document written in Arabic and had Ms. Benz sign the document.  Mr.
Zangana says it is an agreement to marry.  Initially Mr. Zangana told Ms. Benz
that they would be married in his Mosque, and then the necessary papers would
be filed to make the marriage "legal" in Canada.  Mr. Zangana says
that Ms. Benz would not agree to be married in this way.   Ms. Benz says she
was prepared to go through the ceremony proposed by Mr. Zangana, so long as the
marriage was actually registered as a "legal" marriage, but that Mr.
Zangana kept refusing to proceed, and that he never actually asked her to go to
the Mosque to be married.  He did, however, refer to her as "his wife"
after she signed the document written in Arabic.

The evidence of both Mr. Zangana
and Ms. Benz reveals that they actually lived together for only two or three
months in 1991, and with the exception of the first couple of months they were
together, their relationship has been a disaster.

Ms. Benz says that in September,
1991, Mr. Zangana told her he needed to send some money to his family.  Ms.
Benz and Mr. Zangana agreed to apply for social assistance, although both were
working full-time as taxi-drivers, and they began to collect social
assistance.

By October, 1991, the couple had
begun to have angry disputes.  Ms. Benz says Mr. Zangana spat in her face,
pulled her hair, and called her a slut.  There was an incident when Ms. Benz
was seeing a tailoring customer and Mr. Zangana interrupted them.  Ms. Benz
shouted at Mr. Zangana after the customer left and slapped him.  He slapped her
back and both struck the other several times.

In the second or third week of
October, 1991, Ms. Benz learned that she was pregnant with Mr. Zangana's
child.  On October 22 the couple had a bad argument, and Ms. Benz moved out for
a week.  An ultrasound examination on October 23 revealed that the fetus was
not developing properly, and on November 6, 1991, Ms. Benz miscarried.

At the end of November, 1991, the
couple moved from Ms. Benz's friend's townhouse to an apartment in downtown
Winnipeg.  Ms. Benz says that by this time, Mr. Zangana had become quite
violent towards her; slapping and threatening her, as well as verbally abusing
her on a regular basis.

On December 31, 1991, the couple
had a serious argument in their apartment.  Ms. Benz left, but eventually
returned to the apartment after Mr. Zangana had gone to work.  She packed a bag
and went to a women's shelter she had visited before, near the apartment.  Mr.
Zangana came to the shelter looking for her a couple of times.  Ms. Benz
eventually called the police and reported that Mr. Zangana had assaulted her.
Mr. Zangana was charged with having assaulted Ms. Benz on December 31, 1991.
He was released on his own recognizance on condition that he have no contact or
communication with Ms. Benz.

On the recommendation of the
women's shelter staff, Ms. Benz took a bus to Selkirk, Manitoba, and spent four
days at a women's shelter there.  When she returned to Winnipeg she had decided
to stop living with Mr. Zangana.  She stayed in a hotel for about a week.
While staying there, she called Social Services and reported that both she and
Mr. Zangana had been working full-time while they were in receipt of social
assistance.

After December 31, 1991 Ms. Benz
and Mr. Zangana never lived together again, although their relationship
continued in some form or another until October, 1993.  Around January 15,
1992, Ms. Benz found her own apartment.  Sometime in January,  Mr. Zangana
telephoned Ms. Benz.  She reported this contact and a later approach to the
police and Mr. Zangana was charged with a breach of recognizance on January 20,
1992 and again on January 26, 1992.  In March he pursued her taxi with his; she
called the police and he was arrested and again charged with a breach of
recognizance on March 3.  One of the tenants in her apartment building also
called the police after Mr. Zangana was seen driving up and down the lane behind
the building late at night.

Around April, 1992, Mr. Zangana
sent a friend with a gift for Ms. Benz.  A short while later, the couple
reconciled.  Ms. Benz says she felt sorry for him.  She says he begged her not
to testify at his trial on the criminal charges, because a conviction could
interfere with his application for Canadian citizenship.  In July, 1992, Ms.
Benz refused to testify against Mr. Zangana and the assault charge and breach
of recognizance charges were dismissed.

Sometime in late August or early
September, 1992, the couple had another violent argument, and Ms. Benz says Mr.
Zangana kicked her during this argument.

Mr. Zangana had decided he wanted
to buy his own taxi.  He asked Ms. Benz to give or lend him $5,000 but she
refused.  He was insistent, she says, and kept asking her for the money.
Eventually she approached some people she knew to see if they would lend money
to Mr. Zangana.  He was angry that she had been talking to people about him
needing money.

On October 1, 1992, Mr. Zangana
was charged with assault with a weapon, and with possession of two weapons, a
bamboo stick and a steel bar.  The alleged victim was also a Winnipeg taxi
driver.   Mr. Zangana says that these charges were the result of a misunderstanding
arising out of some insulting comments made by the alleged victim to Ms. Benz;
that the other driver was actually the owner of the weapons, and that he, Mr.
Zangana, was the victim of the assault, not the perpetrator.  Mr. Zangana says
he,

the other driver and Ms. Benz went for
mediation and the charges against Mr. Zangana were eventually dismissed.

In late October, 1992, Ms. Benz
learned that she was pregnant.  The couple were excited.  In early December,
1992, an ultrasound examination showed the baby was developing well.  Mr.
Zangana accompanied Ms. Benz to the hospital for the ultrasound.  He says it
was the happiest day of his life and Ms. Benz was also happy.  He says that
later Ms. Benz changed and was not the same Ingrid.  He blames the change on
someone named "Ezra", a friend of Ms. Benz who Mr. Zangana says is
Jewish and hates Muslims.  He says that Ms. Benz wanted him to marry her.  He
put her off, telling her he wanted to talk with his family first and arrange a
Muslim ceremony.  She said that unless he married her legally, she would place
the baby for adoption.

Ms. Benz's explanation of the
events following the confirmation of her pregnancy is quite different.  She
says that although Mr. Zangana initially seemed excited and pleased about her
pregnancy, he later became abusive and threatening.  He bought her some
balloons to celebrate the pregnancy, then burst them with a knife.  He swore at
her; left numerous harassing telephone messages on her answering machine; came
by her apartment and banged on her door and shouted and drove by her building
honking his horn.

The evidence clearly establishes
that in December, 1992 and early January 1993, the couple waged a verbal battle
via telephone answering machine.  Ms. Benz admits that she frequently called
Mr. Zangana and left numerous messages on his answering machine.  She also
called the Manitoba Islamic Association, with which Mr. Zangana is associated,
and left many messages there.

Ms. Benz kept the tapes of some
of the messages Mr. Zangana left on her answering machine, and these were
transcribed.  Mr. Zangana was cross-examined about some of the messages and he
admits making the statements recorded.   They are extremely insulting and
derogatory towards Ms. Benz.  Mr. Zangana accused her of various infidelities
and of having given him a sexually-transmitted disease.  He swore at her and
called her demeaning and degrading names.   Mr. Zangana testified that the
entire blame for these exchanges rests with Ms. Benz, who called his mother and
sister "sluts".  He says that he was only retaliating for her insults
to his family.

Ms. Benz says that during an
argument in her apartment in early January, 1993, Mr. Zangana grabbed her,
shook her and held her pressed against a wall.  She started to scream, and some
tenants in her building knocked at her door, so Mr. Zangana left.

The telephone message war continued.
A few days later, Ms. Benz went to Mr. Zangana's apartment.  When he answered
the door, she screamed at him to stop leaving messages.  One of his neighbors
came out and Ms. Benz had an argument with her.  After the neighbor left, Ms.
Benz says Mr. Zangana took a knife, and held it against her abdomen.  She ran
out of the apartment.

Ms. Benz decided to leave
Winnipeg, have her baby and place it for adoption.  On January 20, 1993,
without telling Mr. Zangana what she planned to do, Ms. Benz took a bus to
Vancouver.  When she arrived, Ms. Benz contacted the Hope Pregnancy and
Adoption Services Society, a non-profit society which provides pregnancy
counselling and assistance to expectant parents; adoption counselling to
prospective adopting parents; and also facilitates private adoptions.

Ms. Benz received counselling and
support through Hope Services throughout the remainder of her pregnancy.  She
told them she was fleeing from an abusive and violent relationship with her
baby's father.  She told them she thought he was a danger to her and to her
child.  In the course of obtaining medical records from the hospital in Winnipeg
where she had had the ultrasound examination, Ms. Benz learned that Mr. Zangana
had been making inquiries about her.  She asked the hospital in Winnipeg to
send her medical records but to keep her whereabouts confidential and they
agreed.  She learned from one of her former tenants in Winnipeg that Mr.
Zangana had been knocking on doors in her apartment building and demanding
information about her whereabouts.

Mr. Zangana is not a
"parent" within the meaning of the
British Columbia Adoption Act

and so it was not necessary to obtain his consent to place baby Ingrid for
adoption.   The executive director of Hope Services testified that the agency's
usual practise is to provide counselling and support to both the prospective
mother and father.  Usually, the father becomes involved, if he wishes to do
so, through the expectant mother.  In this case, Ms. Benz clearly did not wish
Mr. Zangana to be involved, and given what she had told the staff of Hope
Services about him, and his abusive behavior towards her, and her fears for her
child, the agency quite understandably made no effort to contact him.

Ms. Benz testified that when she
came to Vancouver she had already decided to place her baby for adoption.  She
wanted the child to grow up in a stable home with two parents.  She felt that
her relationship with Mr. Zangana was over and that his abusive nature posed a
threat to the child.  She was afraid she might miscarry if she stayed in
Winnipeg.  She was concerned that Mr. Zangana might try to take the child to
Egypt.  She was concerned that he had once indicated his approval of the
practise of female circumcision.

Despite her apparent fear of him,
in March, 1993, Ms. Benz telephoned Mr. Zangana.  He told her he was going to
Cairo.  She told him she hoped he didn't come back.  Mr. Zangana went to Egypt
in March or early April and returned to Winnipeg on June 3, 1993.

When it appeared that Ms. Benz's
decision to place her child for adoption was informed and final, she was given
access to Hope Services' profiles of prospective adoptive couples who had gone
through the extensive counselling required by Hope Services, and who had met
their criteria.

Ms. Benz testified that she had
about fifty profiles of couples to choose from.  She established some criteria
for her selection.  She wanted a couple her own age or older, who were stable,
and who were Christian.  She said this was important to her, although she is
not active in any church.  She wanted a couple who didn't live in a city, as
she was afraid that Mr. Zangana might attempt to abduct the child.  Eventually,
Ms. Zangana selected the Does.  She liked the fact that Mr. Doe had been
adopted himself, and that he had dark hair.  She did not allow the Does to be
contacted, however, until after the birth of baby Ingrid, and until after the
waiting period for revocation of her consent under the
Adoption Act
had
passed.

When baby Ingrid was born, Ms.
Benz certified on the birth certificate that the father of baby Ingrid was
"unknown".  This was a false statement, and she knew it.  She
testified she deliberately chose to make a false declaration because she thought
it would help to keep baby Ingrid safe from Mr. Zangana.  No one at Hope
Services was aware that Ms. Benz had completed the birth certificate in this
fashion.

On the eleventh day after baby
Ingrid's birth, Ms. Benz signed the papers allowing baby Ingrid to be placed
for adoption.  Hope Services contacted the Does, and they made arrangements to
pick up baby Ingrid on July 20, 1993.  They also met Ms. Benz.  The Does had
elected an "open adoption".  They agreed that baby Ingrid would be
told about her birth mother and father and allowed to decide, at an appropriate
age, if she wanted to know them.  The Does met with Ms. Benz.  She gave them
some, but limited information about the baby's father.  She told them his first
name was Jalal.  The Does were excited and overwhelmed at their good fortune in
having been selected by Ms. Benz to parent baby Ingrid.  They did not ask for
more information about the baby's father.   They agreed to provide Ms. Benz
with pictures of baby Ingrid, and to write to her of the baby's progress.

Margaret Doe is 39 years old.
She was born in British Columbia and grew up here.  Her parents and four
siblings are a close family.  She describes a happy childhood.  She completed
Grade 12, and worked as a waitress in her home town during high school and
after graduation.  When she was 21 she married and moved to another city where
she also worked as a waitress.  In 1980 she and her first husband separated.
They were divorced in 1984.  After the separation in 1980, Ms. Doe returned to
her home town and took a ten month community college course in office
administration.  She moved away again when she completed the course and worked
as a waitress and part-time receptionist for a chiropractor.  She was
unemployed for about a year and then got a job as a clerk in a pharmacy where
she worked for six years until she quit to look after baby Ingrid in July,
1993.

Ms. Doe met John Doe in 1986
through an adult bible study group led by Mr. Doe.  They dated for about one
and a half years and then married in 1988.

John Doe is 41 years old and has
also lived in British Columbia all his life.  He and his older sister are both
adopted.  Mr. Doe's adoptive father is a doctor on Vancouver Island.  John Doe
recalls a happy childhood.  He graduated from high school, and then worked in a
small soft drink plant owned by a man he'd met through a church youth group.
After a year and a half, Mr. Doe went to college for automotive training.  He
completed the course and his apprenticeship and qualified as a certified
mechanic in 1976.  In the meantime, Mr. Doe had married and he and his first
wife moved to the town where Margaret and John Doe now live.  Mr. Doe separated
from his first wife in 1982 and they were divorced in 1986.  He met Margaret
Doe not long after.  Mr. Doe works as an auto mechanic and in the winter earns
extra income by driving a snowplow.

During the first two years of
their marriage, the Does didn't concern themselves about having a child, but
then they began to investigate their options.  Ms. Doe had had an ectopic
pregnancy in 1980 and had later had surgery.  In February, 1990 she was advised
that because of scarring, her chances of becoming pregnant, even after another
surgery, were only 15%.  The couple were disappointed.  They wanted a family.
After a year, they started to talk about adoption.  They heard about Hope
Adoption Services and wrote for information.  They received a letter and some
brochures.  Eventually they registered for a one-day seminar sponsored by Hope
Services dealing with infertility, grieving, and the legal aspects of
adoption.  They attended a second, longer seminar about a month later.  They
considered open adoption, and decided that option, involving exchange of
information with the birth mother and father, was best for them.  This was
partly influenced by John's reaction to the information presented at the
seminars about open adoption, and the fact that his sister had made efforts to
locate her birth parents.  After John and Margaret attended the seminars at
Hope Services, John made inquiries to attempt to locate his own birth mother.
He learned that she had died, but he was able to establish contact with his
half-siblings.

Having decided on adoption, the
Does began a lengthy process to register as adoptive parents with Hope
Services.  In addition to the seminars they attended, they had to complete a
24-page questionnaire, were interviewed by the director of Hope Services,
underwent a psychological profile test to determine compatibility  and had a
six hour home study prepared by a qualified social worker.  By February, 1992
they had completed all the necessary steps and were placed on the active
profile list of Hope Services.  After that date they occasionally updated the
photographs and information in their profile and kept in touch with the
agency.

On July 19, 1993 the Does
received a call from Hope Services notifying them that Ingrid Benz has chosen
them to parent baby Ingrid.  They travelled to Vancouver on July 20, met Ingrid
Benz on July 21, and returned home with baby Ingrid that day.

Ingrid Benz returned to Winnipeg
at the end of July, 1993, and shortly after her return, in the second week of
August, she and Mr. Zangana re-established a sexual relationship.  Ms. Benz
told Mr. Zangana that she'd had a child and that it was healthy and strong.
She refused to tell him where the child was.

In August, 1993, Mr. Zangana
applied for legal aid to hire a lawyer in Winnipeg to help him attempt to
locate baby Ingrid and apply for custody of her.

Mr. Zangana and Ms. Benz
continued to see each other but the situation was highly charged.  Ms. Benz
delivered a picture of baby Ingrid with the words "Muslim bastard"
scrawled on it to Mr. Zangana at his work place, along with a "fake"
cheque for $5,000; a reference to the money he had tried to borrow from her the
previous fall.  One time when he was at her apartment he read some cards she
had received when the baby was born and found a card from the Does.  Ms. Benz
admitted she had placed the baby for adoption.

On August 21, 1993 Mr. Zangana
went to Egypt.  He says his brother in Sweden told him his mother was ill, but
in fact it was his brother who was ill, and he died before Mr. Zangana's
arrival.  He returned to Winnipeg on September 6, 1993.  Ms. Benz's letters to
the Does, which are in evidence, indicate that during the late summer and fall
of 1993, Ms. Benz was attempting to stall off Mr. Zangana.  She thought that if
she could keep Mr. Zangana from finding out where the baby was for six months,
all his rights would be lost.  For his part, Mr. Zangana tried to convince Ms.
Benz that he would marry her if she would tell him where the baby was.  Ms.
Benz saw through this ruse.

In fact, Mr. Zangana has
testified that in October, 1993, he arranged to marry Hekmat Amin El-Sayed, an
Egyptian woman he had known, through his friendship with her family, since
1980.  Ms. El-Sayed had separated from her first husband in 1993, and had given
birth to a son in June, 1993.  Mr. Zangana had visited with Ms. El-Sayed's family
and had seen her during his trips to Egypt in April, and in August of 1993.  He
had broached the subject of marriage with Ms. El-Sayed during his trip in
August.  Mr. Zangana says that Ms. El-Sayed agreed in October to marry him when
her divorce was final, and to immigrate from Egypt to Canada, although Mr.
Zangana says that this means, under Egyptian law, that she will have to give up
custody of her infant son to her former husband.  Ms. El-Sayed knew of Mr.
Zangana's desire to locate and obtain custody of baby Ingrid when she agreed to
marry him.

On his return to Canada from
Egypt in September, 1993, Mr. Zangana retained a lawyer in Winnipeg and filed a
petition seeking custody of the child.  On September 28, 1993, Ms. Benz was
ordered by a Justice of the Manitoba Court of Queen's Bench to disclose to Mr.
Zangana's lawyer the name of the child, the gender and date of birth, and
whether the child had been adopted or placed for adoption.

Despite these proceedings, Mr.
Zangana and Ms. Benz continued a relationship of sorts.  In October, Ms. Benz
became incensed when Mr. Zangana allowed a friend to interrupt their dinner.
She threw photographs of baby Ingrid on the table in front of Mr. Zangana and
his friend, spat at them, yelled "Muslim bastard" and ran out of the
apartment.  She smashed windows in Mr. Zangana's apartment.  The police were
called and Ms. Benz was charged with assault on Mr. Zangana and his friend, and
mischief.  She was ordered to have no contact with Mr. Zangana.  After the
incident in October, the relationship between Mr. Zangana and Ms. Benz ended.

In November, 1993, Ms. Benz was
charged with a breach of recognizance for allegedly contacting Mr. Zangana and
threatening to shoot him.  She was held in custody for twelve days at a remand
centre in Winnipeg, and was released on November 15.  Eventually she pleaded
guilty to the mischief charge and one count of breach of recognizance and the
balance of the charges were stayed.

On December l, 1993, Ms. Benz
was ordered by the Manitoba Court of Queen's Bench to disclose to Mr. Zangana's
lawyer within seven days the present whereabouts of the child, the names of the
prospective adopting parents and their address, and the names of any agencies
dealing with the prospective adopting parents.  Ms. Benz failed to do so.  At a
hearing to determine whether she should be cited for contempt and on the advice
of her counsel, she agreed to disclose the name of Hope Services.

Through Hope Services, Mr.
Zangana learned that baby Ingrid had been placed for adoption in British
Columbia.  He came to Vancouver in January, 1994 and filed a petition on
January 14, 1994 seeking custody of baby Ingrid.

The claim against Hope Pregnancy
and Adoption Services Society was dismissed by Master Tokarek of this court on
January 28, 1994.  On February 4, 1994 Justice Koenigsberg ordered that Ms.
Benz be served with notice of Mr. Zangana's application for custody.  After she
was served, Ms. Benz filed her own petition seeking custody of baby Ingrid,
although her primary position continues to be that the Does should have
custody.

On February 7, Justice
Koenigsberg ordered that Mr. Zangana have supervised access to baby Ingrid for
one two-hour session or two one-hour sessions.  He visited with baby Ingrid in
the presence of the Does and a supervisor for two hours in February.

On February 24, 1994 Justice
Williamson ordered that the Does have interim custody of baby Ingrid pending
trial.

In March Mr. Zangana went to
Egypt for the purpose of marrying Ms. El-Sayed.  When he arrived there,
however, the couple learned that under the applicable law, she was not free to
marry for a further period of months.  Mr. Zangana has appointed an attorney to
complete his marriage to Ms. El-Sayed when the requisite time has passed.  He
expects the marriage can be concluded by the end of June after which he will
apply to sponsor Ms. El-Sayed's immigration to Canada.  He expects this will
take at least three months and that Ms. El-Sayed will be able to come to Canada
in September.

Until Ms. El-Sayed arrives, Mr.
Zangana says that some friends and neighbors have offered to assist him in
caring for baby Ingrid in Winnipeg.  Although he does not have a home there
now, he will rent an apartment when he returns to Winnipeg.  He expects to
receive some money, perhaps as much as $10,000, from the settlement of two
motor vehicle accident injury claims, and may use those funds to put a down
payment on a home.  He says that his brother in Sweden has agreed to lend him
the money to purchase his own taxi-cab, if he is given custody of baby Ingrid,
and that he will work as an owner-operator, driving the taxi himself during the
day, and leasing it out at night.  Until he is able to buy his own cab, he will
drive for Unicity Taxi, who have given him a good reference, and he hopes to
get a job driving a van for passengers who are handicapped, an option he was
exploring before he left Winnipeg in January.

Mr. Zangana anticipates that Ms.
El-Sayed will have no difficulty adjusting to her new life with him in
Winnipeg, although she will be leaving behind the relatively affluent
surroundings of her father's home in Egypt, and despite the fact that she will
be giving up custody of her own son in order to marry Mr. Zangana.

Mr. Zangana says he is fully
capable of providing care for baby Ingrid.  He says he cared for his younger
siblings when he was a teenager in Iraq.  He is prepared to take courses in
parenting if necessary.  He would rely on a doctor's advice about what to feed
baby Ingrid, in addition to commercial baby food, if she is placed in his
custody.

Once Ms. El-Sayed arrives, she
will assume the primary responsibility for baby Ingrid's care, as she will not
be working outside the home.  Mr. Zangana plans to raise baby Ingrid as a
Muslim, but says that when she is old enough, she is free to choose any religion
she likes.

During his access visit with baby
Ingrid, Mr. Zangana was able to establish a good rapport.  He bought toys for
her and played with her.  She fussed when the visit was over and he returned
her to Margaret Doe.

In 1990, Mr. Zangana reported
total income of $5,858.  In 1991 he reported income of only $354.  In 1992 he
reported total income of $7,468.  Mr. Zangana testified that these tax returns
accurately reflected his total income in those years.

Mr. Zangana has made friends in
Winnipeg.  He is active in the Islamic community in Winnipeg and in the Kurdish
Association of Manitoba.

Ms. Benz is currently employed in
Winnipeg as the driver of a van for passengers with wheelchairs.  She drives on
day-shift, Tuesday to Friday.  On Sundays she drives taxi part-time for Unicity
Taxi.  She makes $900 to $1,000 gross per month from these jobs and an
additional $20 to $50 a month from her clothing alterations business.  Based on
her evidence, this income is adequate to meet her rent and other expenses,
considering the lower cost of living in Winnipeg.  She plans to enrol in
September, 1994 in a two-year course in apparel design offered part-time at the
University of Manitoba.  She rents a one bedroom suite in a house near downtown
Winnipeg.  She says she has $17,000 in mutual funds, and no debts of any
consequence.  Although she strongly supports the Does' claim to custody, if she
is given custody of baby Ingrid, she says she plans to move into a cooperative
housing complex in northern Winnipeg.  She says that other residents of the
co-op or friends will care for baby Ingrid while she is at work.  Ms. Benz is
not close to her family and has little or no contact with them but she has
friends in Winnipeg.

The Does live in a 22-year-old,
1200 square foot, four-bedroom home, with a fenced back yard, which they bought
five years ago and in which they now have approximately $60,000 in equity.
They had to re-mortgage the home recently to pay legal fees for these
proceedings.  The home is located in a well-established neighborhood, close to
schools and parks, in a city of about 20,000 people.  Ms. Doe quit working
outside the home when baby Ingrid came to live with them.  As a clerk in the
pharmacy she earned $1,200 a month.   Mr. Doe works as an auto-mechanic and
earns $2,200 gross each month plus about $1,000 more in winter for driving a
snowplow.  He works days, Tuesday to Saturday.  Aside from the equity in their
home, the Does have about $9,000 in registered retirement savings and another
$2,000 in savings.

The Does are both close to their
extended families and the extended family are fond of baby Ingrid, especially
Ms. Doe's parents.  The Does are very active in their church and have many
friends.  They like to hike and take drives with baby Ingrid in the country on
weekends and recently took her out in a boat.  They visit with friends and family.

In 1992, after the Does had
registered as adoptive parents with Hope Services, they decorated a room in
their home for a child, and purchased children's furnishings.  As part of the
preparation for becoming adoptive parents, they read extensively, and a list of
the books they read on adoption and child-rearing is in evidence.  The Does
describe baby Ingrid as a happy, easy-going child who slept through the night
soon after her arrival.  She has had some colds but no real health problems.

POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES

Mr. Zangana primarily advances
his claim to custody on the grounds of the blood relationship between himself
and baby Ingrid.  He concedes that the Does are competent parents who care for
baby Ingrid and are capable of providing her with a good home.  He asserts that
he is equally capable of parenting baby Ingrid, and that where the scales are
equally balanced with respect to the best interests of the child, the natural
parent's claim should prevail.  He has been vigilant in advancing his claim for
custody.  He took steps to try to locate Ms. Benz when she left Winnipeg in
January, 1993, and brought his claim for custody of baby Ingrid as soon as he
learned where she was.  He denies the allegations of physical abuse and
violence made by Ms. Benz.  He says that while she was violent towards him, he
did not reciprocate and that his verbal abuse was merely a response to her
insulting statements.  He intends to raise baby Ingrid in his religion and
familiarize her with his cultural heritage, in a traditional, family-oriented
home, with the assistance of Ms. El-Sayed, who has expressed her interest, in
her affidavit, in caring for baby Ingrid.  He says that if he is given custody
of baby Ingrid, his brother in Sweden will assist him to buy his own taxi-cab
and that he will be able to earn enough to support himself and his wife and
baby Ingrid as an owner-operator.   Although he does not dispute that baby
Ingrid has formed an attachment to the Does, he says that she will adjust,
particularly if the Does assist by making her clothing and familiar possessions
available to him.

The Does say that baby Ingrid is
happy, secure and comfortable in the only home she has ever known, with the
only parents she has ever known, and has bonded with them, and their extended
family and friends.  While they have modest financial means, they have planned
and organized their lives to make a stable and secure home for themselves and a
child.  They plan to raise baby Ingrid in a traditional home, with an emphasis
on Christian religious values and morals.  They are familiar with her physical
and emotional needs, and have been meeting those needs for nine months.  They
say they are a mature couple, compatible, and committed to each other and to
their marriage.

The Does, through their counsel,
question the depth of Mr. Zangana's commitment to baby Ingrid's best
interests.  The Does say that Mr. Zangana, during his access visit, asked no
questions about baby Ingrid and the first nine months of her life.  They  query
whether Mr. Zangana fully understands what being responsible for the care of an
infant involves.

The Does are concerned that Mr.
Zangana's relationship with Ms. Benz and his conduct towards her demonstrate
that he may not be capable of providing the emotional support and appropriate
guidance that baby Ingrid will require as she grows to adulthood.

Ms. Benz continues to adhere to
the decision she made in July, 1993 and supports the Does' claim for continuing
custody of baby Ingrid.  She says, however, that if the court is of the view
that one of baby Ingrid's birth parents should have custody of her, then Ms.
Benz is the appropriate parent.  She says that she is financially able to
provide for baby Ingrid, and that Mr. Zangana is not.  She says that Mr.
Zangana's abusive and violent nature makes him an unfit parent, and that the
attitudes he has displayed towards her and toward women in general are of
particular concern given that this child is a girl.  She says that Mr. Zangana
was violent and abusive towards her, even when she was pregnant with baby
Ingrid.  She says that Mr. Zangana lacks the financial resources to properly
provide for baby Ingrid, and that he under-estimates the difficulty in being
the owner-operator of a taxi.

THE LAW

Section 24 of the
Family Relations
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1979, c.121, as amended, establishes that in making a custody
or access order, a court in British Columbia shall give paramount consideration
to the best interests of the child.  In assessing these interests, the court
shall consider the health and emotional well-being of the child, the love,
affection and similar ties that exist between the child and other persons,
education and training for the child and the capacity of each person seeking
custody or access to exercise the rights of custody or access adequately.  The
conduct of a person applying for custody or access is to be considered only
where that conduct affects one of the factors set out above, and only to the
extent that the conduct affects one of those factors.

Section 27 of the
Family
Relations Act
establishes that Ms. Benz was the sole guardian of baby
Ingrid at the time of her birth, since she and Mr. Zangana were not married to
each other and had not lived together since December, 1991.  She had the legal
right to place baby Ingrid for adoption and she did not require Mr. Zangana's
consent to do so.  Neither Hope Services not the Does were obliged by law to
contact him, or to obtain his consent.  They were entitled to rely on the
consent to adoption of Ms. Benz as baby Ingrid's sole guardian.

Mr. Zangana is not a
"parent" in relation to baby Ingrid, as that term is defined in the
Family
Relations Act
.  Mr. Zangana concedes that he is also not a
"parent" as that term is defined under the
Adoption Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1979, c.4, and that he was not a "parent" under that
Act

at the time that baby Ingrid was placed for adoption by Ms. Benz.

Nevertheless, Mr. Zangana is a
person entitled to seek custody of or access to baby Ingrid.  He has
acknowledged paternity.  If he is awarded custody or if an order is made for
access, he will acquire the status of "parent" under s.8(d) of the
Adoption
Act
which provides that parent includes "a man who has acknowledged
paternity and who has custody or access rights by court order or agreement".

In
K.K. v. G.L. and B.J.L.
,

(1985)
1985 CanLII 59 (SCC)
,
44 R.F.L. (2d) 113
, the Supreme Court of Canada provided guidance in
determining the best interests of a child in a contest over custody between the
birth mother, who had revoked her consent to adoption, and the adoptive
parents.  At p.119 of the reasons, McIntyre, J., speaking for the court,
discussed the evolution of the law relating to custody in the following
passage:

"The
law relating to the custody of children and the rights of parents where custody
claims are involved has undergone progressive change since early in the
nineteenth century when the parent, usually the father, had a right to custody
of an infant child unless dis-qualified by reason of some serious circumstance
having to do with the welfare of the child, making him unfit to have custody.
By legislative intervention and evolving case law the situation has changed.
The law has moved, first, toward an increase in maternal rights; a progressive
diminution of parental rights; and then, a corresponding increase in the
consideration of the interest or welfare of the infant, as the significant
factor in custody determination. This latter factor has become progressively
more important until it may now be said that the welfare of the child is the
paramount consideration when the courts address the problem."

Later in the reasons, Justice
McIntyre says that there has been a significant move in the law away from
reliance upon the parental preference.  He referred to the decision of Wilson,
J. speaking for the Supreme Court of Canada in
A.N.R. and S.C.R. v. L.J.W.
,
(1983) 36 R.F.L. (2d) l.  This was a case involving a contest over custody and
adoption between a birth mother and adoptive parents.  In that case, the
Supreme Court restored the order of the trial judge approving an adoption over
the objections of the birth mother who was seeking to regain custody.  Justice
Wilson said that a child's tie with its natural parent is very relevant in a
determination as to what is in a child's best interests.   However, at p.11 of
her reasons she also said:

"But
it is the parental tie as a meaningful and positive force in the life of the
child and not in the life of the parent that the court has to be concerned
about. As has been emphasized many time in custody cases, a child is not a
chattel in which its parents have a proprietary interest; it is a human being
to whom they owe serious obligations."

At p.126 of
the reasons in
K.K.
,
Justice McIntyre reiterated that all other considerations must remain
subordinate to a consideration of what is in the best interests of the child.
He also said:

"This
is not to say that the question of custody will be determined by weighing the
economic circumstances of the contending parties.  The matter will not be
determined solely on the basis of the physical comfort and material advantages
that may be available in the home of one contender or the other. The welfare of
the child must be considered on a consideration of these and all other relevant
factors, including the general psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare
of the child. It must be the aim of the court, when resolving disputes between
rival claimants for the custody of a child, to choose the course which will
best provide for the healthy growth, development and education of the child so
that he will be equipped to face the problems of life as a mature adult.
Parental claims must not be lightly set aside, and they are entitled to serious
consideration in reaching any conclusion. Where it is clear that the welfare of
the child requires it, however, they must be set aside."

Although s.24 of the
Family
Relations Act
makes no reference to consideration of a blood relationship,
the British Columbia Court of Appeal held in
M.(C.G.) v. W.(C.)[B.C.]
,

(1989)
1989 CanLII 5232 (BC CA)
,
23 R.F.L. (3d) 1
, that at least on an application for interim custody,
where the scales between a natural father and prospective adoptive parents are
otherwise equally balanced, the natural parent's claim for custody should
prevail.  In that case, the application for custody was brought by the natural
father and his parents jointly.

Justice Cowan also appeared to
recognize a presumption in favor of custody to birth parents in
W.(L.G.) v.
W.(H.).
, (1989)

1989 CanLII 2951 (BC SC)
,
22 R.F.L. (3d), 362
.  In that case,
the birth parents, who were not married, agreed to place their child for
adoption six days after its birth.  Two days later they sought to revoke their
consent and asked for the return of the child.  A few days after that they
filed a petition seeking custody.  On the facts before him, Justice Cowan felt
the circumstances surrounding the consent to adoption had to be given great
weight.  He held that the birth parents should not be deprived of the
opportunity of making a life for their child.  He set aside the parents'
consent to adoption and returned the child to their custody.

Justice Prowse, sitting in B.C.
Supreme Court, also addressed the question of the significance of blood ties in
a case in which the birth mother of a fifteen month old child sought to revoke
her consent to an adoption.  This decision,
In the Matter of a Male Infant,
British Columbia Birth Registration Number 030279
, Vancouver Registry
A890789, January 23, 1990, is apparently unreported.  In her reasons, Justice
Prowse indicated that she had given serious consideration to the factor of
blood ties, bearing in mind that some of the benefits that flow to a child from
blood ties are "intangible, and not readily put into words".  On the
facts before her, she concluded that the best interests of the child dictated
that the birth mother's consent to adoption should not be set aside, and the
adoptive parents should retain custody, even when blood ties, combined with
other factors favouring the natural mother were considered.

In the authorities proffered by
counsel, consideration is also given to the weight to be given to the bond
which may have developed between adoptive custodial parents and the child whose
welfare is in issue.  Bonding between the non-birth parents and the child in
their custody is often discussed in conjunction with a consideration of the
"known" environment versus the "unknown" environment
offered by the birth parent seeking to gain or regain custody.  In Justice
Prowse's decision, referred to above, she addresses these factors.  In that
case, the child had been with the adoptive parents for thirteen months.
Justice Prowse found that the child had bonded with all members of the adoptive
family during that period, and that the natural mother was a virtual stranger
to the child.  Ultimately she held that the most compelling factor in favor of
leaving the child with the adoptive parents was that the child was safe,
secure, happy and healthy in his present environment.

In
Tearoe v. Sawan
, an
unreported decision of the British Columbia Court of Appeal, Victoria Registry
No. V01916, August 19, 1993, (leave to the Supreme Court of Canada denied),
Justice Proudfoot speaking for the court also discussed the issue of bonding
between an eighteen month old child and his adoptive parents.  The birth mother
had cared for the child for less than a month after its birth, and had visited
the child in a foster home a few times before the child was two months old.
The court held that it would not be in the child's best interests to disrupt
him from his present environment and to put him through the uncertainty
associated with an attempt to establish a bond with his birth mother.  Justice
Proudfoot said that while it was quite possible that the birth mother could
also provide a loving environment in

which the child could thrive, to place
him with her was to expose him to an uncertain future that would take away from
him the continuity and stability he enjoyed with his adoptive parents.  She
held that the factors favoring custody in the adoptive parents outweighed both
the blood tie of the birth mother, a native person, and her desire to raise the
child, whose birth father was non-native, in the Cree culture.

ANALYSIS AND DECISION

I am completely satisfied, in the
circumstances of this case, that baby Ingrid's best interests lie in the
continuing custody of John and Margaret Doe.  This is not a case where all
other factors are equal, and the presumptive claim of the natural parent should
succeed.   In my view, the Does have significantly more to offer baby Ingrid in
terms of her health and emotional well-being, education and training.  Strong
ties of love and affection have formed between the Does, their extended family,
and baby Ingrid.

Baby Ingrid is presently in a
safe, secure and happy home.  Mr. Zangana concedes, and the evidence
establishes, that the Does have been loving and competent parents in the nine
months since baby Ingrid came to live with them.  That baby Ingrid has
"bonded" to her adoptive parents is established by their evidence,
and by the opinion of Dr. Michael Elterman, whose report was filed by counsel
for the Does.  He included in his report a paper written by him on the effects
of separation in child protection cases.  Although written in that context, the
report discusses the effect in general on young children of separation from the
parent they know.  The child may experience fear, despair, depression,
withdrawal and distress.   Depending on the circumstances, the child may show
lasting negative effects of this disruption.

Although I accept that Mr.
Zangana cares about baby Ingrid, and that he believes that he has her best
interests at heart, I am not satisfied that he has carefully thought through
the very onerous responsibility involved in caring for a young child.  He
appears to have only a superficial understanding of the potential effect a
complete change in caregiver and environment might mean for her.  To award
custody of baby Ingrid to Mr. Zangana would mean removing her from a known
situation of security and stability to a situation with many unknowns.

Mr. Zangana presently has no
residence in Winnipeg, and the exact identity and circumstances of the persons
whom Mr. Zangana suggests would provide care for baby Ingrid until his future
wife arrives in Canada, are also unknown.  Unfortunately, the court had no
opportunity to assess Ms. El-Sayed's parenting abilities, since she was unable
to come to Canada to testify.  What is known is that when she arrives, she and
Mr. Zangana will be adjusting to a new relationship.  Although they have known
each other for many years, they have spent little time alone together and have
had minimal contact.  She will be leaving behind her own infant son and her
close extended family, to come to a country she does not know and where she
knows no one, other than Mr. Zangana.

Mr. Zangana was unable to provide
a very detailed description of Ms. El-Sayed's personality and interests.  When
asked to describe why Ms. El-Sayed would make a good mother for baby Ingrid, he
answered in terms of her honesty and religious beliefs, but primarily
emphasized that she will be a good wife because she loves him and will not be
unfaithful to him.  Although he is anxious to gain custody of his own daughter,
whom he has seen only once, Mr. Zangana expects that Ms. El-Sayed will have
little difficulty adjusting to leaving her own infant behind in Egypt.  In
general, he gave this child no consideration.  In fact, at his examination for
discovery on March 4, 1994, months after he had become engaged to Ms. El-Sayed
and only days before he planned to leave for Egypt to marry her, he could not
recall the name of her son.

Although the Does are not
financially well-off by any means, they have planned and organized their
finances in a way that enables them to provide a secure and stable environment
for baby Ingrid.  They own a home and a vehicle.  They have some savings for
emergencies.  Mr. Zangana's ability to provide for baby Ingrid and his new
wife, at least in the short term, is questionable.  While social assistance may
be available to him, he did not testify to any inquiries in this regard.  He
did not appear to have a plan of any kind to obtain the necessary funds, in the
short term, to establish a home for himself and baby Ingrid in Winnipeg, and to
meet the expenses of child-care, medical care, food, clothes and furniture for
a growing infant.  He did testify that Ms. El-Sayed will be bringing some money
with her from Egypt, but emphasized that this will be kept for future contingencies,
and, in any event, she will not be coming to Canada for several months.

Although Mr. Zangana embarked on
a home-study initiated by Manitoba's Social Services Ministry at the request of
the British Columbia Ministry, he did not follow through to have the study
completed once he had moved to British Columbia.  While Mr. Zangana may be at a
disadvantage in not having had any opportunity to actually demonstrate his
ability to parent baby Ingrid, he also offered the court no independent
evidence about himself, his character, or his understanding of parental
responsibilities, aside from a reference from his last employer.

I am also concerned that while
Mr. Zangana asserts a belief in "traditional values", his actions
towards Ms. Benz and other conduct in his past contradict these assertions, and
call into question his ability to provide the kind of psychological and
emotional support and role model that baby Ingrid will require to grow into an
emotionally healthy adult.   Mr. Zangana was not willing to marry Ms. Benz,
despite her desire to marry him, even when she became pregnant for a second
time.  There is no evidence that he would or could have supported and helped
her if she chose to keep her child.  Had she returned to Winnipeg before the
birth of her child, she would have found that Mr. Zangana had gone to Egypt for
two months.

At the very least, Mr. Zangana
was verbally abusive towards Ms. Benz during their prolonged unhealthy
relationship, as she was towards him.   Both demonstrated a lack of ability to
resolve conflict and to communicate in a mature and responsible fashion.  Both
were charged with criminal offences as a result.

In general, I prefer the evidence
of Ms. Benz where it conflicts with that of Mr. Zangana.  I accept the evidence
of Ms. Benz that the conflict between herself and Mr. Zangana did escalate into
episodes of mutual physical violence, and that Mr. Zangana struck her,
threatened her, and physically abused her before and during her pregnancy.
Despite Ms. Benz's admission that she made a false declaration on baby Ingrid's
birth certificate, and that she was prepared to disobey a Manitoba court order
in order to keep baby Ingrid's whereabouts a secret from Mr. Zangana, she had a
peculiarly honest approach to her evidence in this court that I found
compelling and believable.  She clearly has her own moral code, but I accept
that she was telling the truth when she testified before me.  She was quite
prepared to admit the full extent of her own violent and illegal behavior.  She
did not attempt to minimize her own actions.  She was frank and on occasion,
startlingly forthright, when it would have been possible and in her own
interests for her to be otherwise.  Her evidence was consistent and she was
unshaken in cross-examination, although I do accept that she probably converted
her belief that Mr. Zangana would take the baby back to Egypt into a statement
that he had specifically threatened to do so.  She freely admitted she was
angry at Mr. Zangana for his conduct towards her and frustrated by his refusal
to marry her.  She said she was not afraid for herself, however, or motivated
by malice when she left for Vancouver.  She testified that she only left
Winnipeg when Mr. Zangana had given her good reason to fear that his violent actions
would harm her child, or possibly result in a miscarriage.  This evidence is
consistent with her behavior, and with the information she provided to staff at
Hope Services.

Mr. Zangana's evidence, on the
other hand, was often self-serving.  He blamed Ms. Benz entirely for the
conflicts between them.  He says, in effect, "she asked for it".  He
denied all violence toward her and others.  He accepted no responsibility for
continuing their unhealthy and potentially explosive relationship.  Although called
in reply at the conclusion of the respondents' case, he provided no explanation
for his participation in the scheme to collect social assistance while working
full-time.  He claimed that he had accurately reported his income to Revenue
Canada in 1991, when it is clearly impossible to survive an entire year, even
in Winnipeg, on $354.  He emphasized, throughout his testimony, the wrongs he
conceived had been done to him; by Ms. Benz, by Hope Services, by the Does; and
what he perceived as a conspiracy to deny him his rights.  This was his focus,
rather than the best interests of baby Ingrid.

While the benefit to a child of
being raised by his or her biological parent is real, even if intangible, this
benefit may be out-weighed by other factors.  In this case, Mr. Zangana has
emphasized his desire to have baby Ingrid raised in the religious and cultural
heritage of her biological father. But baby Ingrid's biological mother has
expressed her own preferences, as she was entitled as sole guardian to do, in
the selection of the Does to be baby Ingrid's adoptive parents.  Ms. Benz's
religious and cultural heritage is different from Mr. Zangana's.  The divergent
religious views and cultural heritage of both parents cannot be accommodated.
If either Mr. Zangana or Ms. Benz had custody of baby Ingrid, it is also highly
probable that conflict between them, and possibly violent confrontations, would
occur.

In many ways, however, the Does
demonstrate an adherence to the kinds of so-called traditional religious and
moral values that Mr. Zangana supports.  Ms. Doe has chosen to work at home,
looking after baby Ingrid.  The Does live a quiet family, church and
community-oriented life; the kind of life Mr. Zangana says he would like baby
Ingrid to have.

Despite the misgivings I have
about Mr. Zangana's ability to put baby Ingrid's best interests ahead of his
own, I suppose it is possible that Mr. Zangana, together with his new wife,
could offer baby Ingrid a happy and secure childhood and an opportunity to
prepare herself to meet the challenges of adulthood.  But this is a risk that
baby Ingrid is not obliged to take.  No one can predict the future.  But the
parents chosen by Ms. Benz to raise the child she gave birth to are stable,
mature and loving.  They have demonstrated maturity, and responsibility in
their lives, and in their care for the child they have had in their custody for
the past nine months.  To disrupt baby Ingrid's relationship with the Does and
their extended family and friends and to place her in a situation where the
future is much more uncertain is not warranted here.  The best interests of
baby Ingrid dictate that she remain in the custody of the Does.  The petitions
of Mr. Zangana and Ms. Benz for custody of baby Ingrid are therefore dismissed.

ACCESS

Mr. Zangana has asked that he be
granted access to baby Ingrid if he is not awarded custody.  However, it is has
not been established that baby Ingrid would benefit from access to her
biological father at this time.  The Does have decided that their adoption of
baby Ingrid will be an "open adoption".  Mr. Doe testified that they
will tell baby Ingrid that she is adopted, and who her birth parents are.  When
she is old enough to make an informed decision about whether she wishes to be
in contact with her birth parents, the Does are prepared to facilitate that
contact.  They have agreed to keep Ms. Benz informed, for a specific period,
about baby Ingrid's progress, and they are prepared to do the same for Mr.
Zangana.

Justice Proudfoot, in
H. and
H. v. Y. and L.
,
(1989)
1989 CanLII 2926 (BC SC)
,
19 R.F.L. (3d) 216
, dealt with the issue of access rights
sought by a natural father after an order granting custody to adoptive parents
had been made.  In that case, there was evidence that the father had some
emotional problems, and Justice Proudfoot ultimately made a restraining order
against him.  However, it is clear from her reasons that the father's emotional
instability was not the primary reason for her refusal to grant access.
Essentially she concluded, as I must here, that there is no evidence that
contact between the child and its natural parent is in the best interests of
the child.  Justice Proudfoot said at p.219:

"Should
Mr. Y be granted access, would this be in the best interests of N? It is only
if it were in her best interests, that it would add something to her life and
her development, happiness and wellbeing, that such an order would be
contemplated. Mr. Y does not know this child and certainly this child has no
knowledge of him.  She is now almost 20 months of age and has spent her entire
life with the H.'s save and except three weeks. She now is thriving, happy and
healthy, has continuity, consistency and stability in her life. What possible
benefit could there be in injecting into this little girl's life yet another
person who maintains he has some proprietary right because he is the natural
father. There is absolutely no evidence before me to convince me that such a
new dimension would add anything to this child's life or be in her best
interests. On the contrary, it could be counter-productive."

There seems to be little doubt
that baby Ingrid enjoyed her visit with Mr. Zangana.  But it is likely that she
would have enjoyed such a visit with any congenial adult who brought her toys
and concentrated on amusing her for a couple of hours.  Mr. Zangana plans to
return to Winnipeg.  The Does do not live in the lower mainland of British
Columbia.  Access would be infrequent and difficult in any event.  I am not
satisfied that there is any evidence that it is in baby Ingrid's best interests
to have contact with Mr. Zangana.  I am confident, particularly given Mr. Doe's
own experience as an adopted child,  and the Does' extensive exposure to
adoption issues through Hope Services, that the Does will sensitively and
fairly introduce baby Ingrid to the fact of her adoption and the identities of
her biological parents in an appropriate way and at an appropriate time.  Even
before the Does were aware of Mr. Zangana's interest in baby Ingrid, they asked
Ms. Benz to provide a photograph of him that they could show baby Ingrid when
she is old enough to understand adoption.  Despite their very natural distress
and apprehension about these proceedings initiated by Mr. Zangana, both
Margaret and John Doe displayed a fair and concerned attitude about Mr. Zangana
and Ms. Benz, overridden only by their concern for baby Ingrid's well-being.
To the extent possible, they tried to avoid choosing sides between Ms. Benz and
Mr. Zangana.  Since baby Ingrid will know who her father is, she can choose, at
the appropriate time, whether to initiate contact with him.

Until then, as Justice Proudfoot
said
in
H. v. Y.
, this is not a case where a relationship between a
natural parent and child should be maintained after custody is given to
others.  There is no relationship to maintain.  Granting access to Mr. Zangana
would merely add another dimension which has not been shown to be in baby
Ingrid's best interests at this time.  The application for access is denied.

I regret that this decision will
no doubt distress Mr. Zangana greatly.  He has diligently pursued what he
perceived to be in baby Ingrid's best interests.  This court has the unenviable
task of deciding such difficult issues, knowing the unhappiness which must
result, but in the hope and confident expectation that this child's best chance
for a secure and happy future has been secured.

"W.G.
Baker, J."

Vancouver, B.C.

April 29, 1994
